text:
The long awaited Lasagna Soup! 🍝 I’m finally getting around to making this viral soup and WOWWW it’s insanely good! It honestly might be my favorite soup of the series! 

Let me know if you make it! Here’s how: 

1/2 yellow onion, diced (about a cup)
6-8 cloves minced garlic, to taste
1/2 lb hot or mild Italian sausage (I used hot)
1/2 lb lean ground beef
2 T tomato paste
Salt and pepper to taste
1-2 t Tony’s Seasoning, to taste
1 t dried basil
1 t dried parsley
1 t dried oregano
1 t Italian seasoning
1/2 t red pepper (to taste)
24 oz marinara
1/2 cup heavy cream
4-6 cups chicken stock, depending on how soupy you want it
1/2 lb Laguna noodles, broken into pieces
Handful of fresh basil

1 cup parm
1 cup ricotta
1 cup mozzarella
1/4 cup fresh parsley
Salt and pepper to taste

1. In a medium bowl, combine your parm, ricotta, mozzarella, parsley, salt and pepper. Set aside.
2. In a large soup pot or dutch oven, heat your olive oil over medium heat. Add in your onion, add a pinch of salt, and cook for 4 minutes.  Throw in your garlic and cook until fragrant, about 30 seconds. 
3. Add in your sausage and beef, breaking into pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook for a few minutes and then season with your salt, pepper, basil, oregano, parsley, Italian, red pepper, and Tony’s. Cook until no longer pink.
4. Add in your tomato paste and stir. Cook for a couple minutes. Pour in your chicken broth and marinara. Bring to a boil. 
5. Pour in your lasagna pieces, reduce heat, and  simmer for about 10 minutes, or until al dente, stirring occasionally. 
6. Once your noodles are done, add in your heavy cream and fresh basil (torn). Adjust seasonings if needed. Stir, serve, and top with a dollop of your ricotta mixture. Enjoy!

text:
The long awaited Lasagna Soup! 🍝 I’m finally getting around to making this viral soup and WOWWW it’s insanely good! It honestly might be my favorite soup of the series! 

Let me know if you make it! Here’s how: 

1/2 yellow onion, diced (about a cup)
6-8 cloves minced garlic, to taste
1/2 lb hot or mild Italian sausage (I used hot)
1/2 lb lean ground beef
2 T tomato paste
Salt and pepper to taste
1-2 t Tony’s Seasoning, to taste
1 t dried basil
1 t dried parsley
1 t dried oregano
1 t Italian seasoning
1/2 t red pepper (to taste)
24 oz marinara
1/2 cup heavy cream
4-6 cups chicken stock, depending on how soupy you want it
1/2 lb Laguna noodles, broken into pieces
Handful of fresh basil

1 cup parm
1 cup ricotta
1 cup mozzarella
1/4 cup fresh parsley
Salt and pepper to taste

1. In a medium bowl, combine your parm, ricotta, mozzarella, parsley, salt and pepper. Set aside.
2. In a large soup pot or dutch oven, heat your olive oil over medium heat. Add in your onion, add a pinch of salt, and cook for 4 minutes.  Throw in your garlic and cook until fragrant, about 30 seconds. 
3. Add in your sausage and beef, breaking into pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook for a few minutes and then season with your salt, pepper, basil, oregano, parsley, Italian, red pepper, and Tony’s. Cook until no longer pink.
4. Add in your tomato paste and stir. Cook for a couple minutes. Pour in your chicken broth and marinara. Bring to a boil. 
5. Pour in your lasagna pieces, reduce heat, and  simmer for about 10 minutes, or until al dente, stirring occasionally. 
6. Once your noodles are done, add in your heavy cream and fresh basil (torn). Adjust seasonings if needed. Stir, serve, and top with a dollop of your ricotta mixture. Enjoy!

text:
When you're ready to start landing paid brand collaborations, knowing how to negotiate and what to look for in contracts is a MUST 💪🏽

Here are some lessons I've learned through doing partnerships over the past five years:

1️⃣ You can say no! – If a brand only offers free products and doesn't have a budget to pay you. It's okay to say no.

Your content takes time, effort, and creativity—you deserve to be compensated fairly.

2️⃣ Know who will "OWN" the content you create – If a brand wants to use your content on organic platforms or for ads, they have to state that in their contract AND they have to pay you for that usage!

3️⃣ Set Boundaries on Usage – If you ever see "perpetuity" in a contract, run the other way 😂 (or ask them to remove it). Basically that's saying the brand will own your content for forever!

Of course everyone will have their own boundaries and standards when doing collabs. For example, if there's a small business you LOVE and you want to work with them, it's normal for small businesses to not have a large budget for paying creators! You could say yes to them if you absolutely want to 😁

💡 Negotiating isn’t “asking for too much”; it’s simply standing up for your worth AND for all the other Creators out there doing the same.

Knowing your rates and boundaries leads to partnerships that respect both you and your work.

💼 What’s the deal with shell companies? 🕵️‍♂️

Shell companies are exactly what they sound like: a shell. They exist on paper but often hide who really owns what. Imagine a company in Wyoming setting up one in Nevada, which then sets up another in California. This web of companies, sometimes called a series LLC, makes it almost impossible for federal departments to track down the real owner.

Why do people use them? To hide assets, dodge taxes, or even cover up shady dealings during divorces or business disputes. It’s been a problem for years.

With agencies like the FBI and banking systems stepping in, there’s hope to bring more transparency to who owns what. But for now… it’s still a mess. 🌀

text:
The long awaited Lasagna Soup! 🍝 I’m finally getting around to making this viral soup and WOWWW it’s insanely good! It honestly might be my favorite soup of the series! 

Let me know if you make it! Here’s how: 

1/2 yellow onion, diced (about a cup)
6-8 cloves minced garlic, to taste
1/2 lb hot or mild Italian sausage (I used hot)
1/2 lb lean ground beef
2 T tomato paste
Salt and pepper to taste
1-2 t Tony’s Seasoning, to taste
1 t dried basil
1 t dried parsley
1 t dried oregano
1 t Italian seasoning
1/2 t red pepper (to taste)
24 oz marinara
1/2 cup heavy cream
4-6 cups chicken stock, depending on how soupy you want it
1/2 lb Laguna noodles, broken into pieces
Handful of fresh basil

1 cup parm
1 cup ricotta
1 cup mozzarella
1/4 cup fresh parsley
Salt and pepper to taste

1. In a medium bowl, combine your parm, ricotta, mozzarella, parsley, salt and pepper. Set aside.
2. In a large soup pot or dutch oven, heat your olive oil over medium heat. Add in your onion, add a pinch of salt, and cook for 4 minutes.  Throw in your garlic and cook until fragrant, about 30 seconds. 
3. Add in your sausage and beef, breaking into pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook for a few minutes and then season with your salt, pepper, basil, oregano, parsley, Italian, red pepper, and Tony’s. Cook until no longer pink.
4. Add in your tomato paste and stir. Cook for a couple minutes. Pour in your chicken broth and marinara. Bring to a boil. 
5. Pour in your lasagna pieces, reduce heat, and  simmer for about 10 minutes, or until al dente, stirring occasionally. 
6. Once your noodles are done, add in your heavy cream and fresh basil (torn). Adjust seasonings if needed. Stir, serve, and top with a dollop of your ricotta mixture. Enjoy!

If you're battling stubborn weeds in your lawn, you've likely heard of herbicides like quinclorac and Trimec Classic. These powerful tools are essential for maintaining a healthy, lush turf, especially when dealing with broadleaf and grassy weeds that just won’t quit. Understanding how to use these products effectively can make all the difference in your lawn care routine.

Quinclorac is particularly effective against tough grassy weeds like crabgrass, which can quickly take over your lawn if left unchecked. This herbicide works by inhibiting the weed’s growth, ultimately causing it to wither and die. It’s a post-emergent solution, meaning it’s best used when the weeds are actively growing. However, timing and application rates are crucial—applying too early or too late can reduce its effectiveness.

On the other hand, Trimec Classic is your go-to for broadleaf weeds such as dandelions, clover, and chickweed. This selective herbicide targets the weeds without harming your grass, making it a reliable choice for a weed-free lawn. When using Trimec Classic, remember to follow the label instructions closely, especially regarding temperature and moisture conditions, to ensure optimal results.

Combining quinclorac and Trimec Classic can give you a comprehensive approach to weed control. However, always remember that these are powerful chemicals, and proper application is key to protecting your lawn and the environment. Five years ago, I was dying.
Alcohol had taken everything—my health, my peace, my hope.
I was clinging to life in a hospital bed, swollen and yellowed, drowning in the consequences of my addiction.
And yet… I am still here.
Because miracles don’t always come in flashes of light.
Sometimes they come in second chances, in the quiet bravery to say "not like this."

I received a liver. A kidney.
But the greatest transplant of all was the one that happened inside me—
when I chose to live.
When I chose to change.

To anyone out there battling addiction or despair—
I was where you are. I know that kind of darkness.
But I promise you, there is a way forward.
You are not too far gone. You are not too broken.
There is beauty waiting for you—
a version of you that you haven’t even met yet.

And they are worth fighting for.

the water screams sublime.

deep breaths, stand back, it’s time.

the safety back at top.

silence drowns the sound.

the view from halfway down.

The long awaited Lasagna Soup! 🍝 I’m finally getting around to making this viral soup and WOWWW it’s insanely good! It honestly might be my favorite soup of the series! 

Let me know if you make it! Here’s how: 

1/2 yellow onion, diced (about a cup)
6-8 cloves minced garlic, to taste
1/2 lb hot or mild Italian sausage (I used hot)
1/2 lb lean ground beef
2 T tomato paste
Salt and pepper to taste
1-2 t Tony’s Seasoning, to taste
1 t dried basil
1 t dried parsley
1 t dried oregano
1 t Italian seasoning
1/2 t red pepper (to taste)
24 oz marinara
1/2 cup heavy cream
4-6 cups chicken stock, depending on how soupy you want it
1/2 lb Laguna noodles, broken into pieces
Handful of fresh basil

1 cup parm
1 cup ricotta
1 cup mozzarella
1/4 cup fresh parsley
Salt and pepper to taste

1. In a medium bowl, combine your parm, ricotta, mozzarella, parsley, salt and pepper. Set aside.
2. In a large soup pot or dutch oven, heat your olive oil over medium heat. Add in your onion, add a pinch of salt, and cook for 4 minutes.  Throw in your garlic and cook until fragrant, about 30 seconds. 
3. Add in your sausage and beef, breaking into pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook for a few minutes and then season with your salt, pepper, basil, oregano, parsley, Italian, red pepper, and Tony’s. Cook until no longer pink.
4. Add in your tomato paste and stir. Cook for a couple minutes. Pour in your chicken broth and marinara. Bring to a boil. 
5. Pour in your lasagna pieces, reduce heat, and  simmer for about 10 minutes, or until al dente, stirring occasionally. 
6. Once your noodles are done, add in your heavy cream and fresh basil (torn). Adjust seasonings if needed. Stir, serve, and top with a dollop of your ricotta mixture. Enjoy!

🎯 Stop playing it safe — explore unconventional grids like a creative pro! Here’s how to master irregular, diagonal, and radial layouts — and when to use each 👇

Forget symmetry for a sec — these grids add energy, movement, and wow to your designs. Here's the breakdown:

🔀 Irregular Grid – Non-uniform, often custom-built based on content. Think controlled chaos with purpose. 🟡 Best for: Editorial spreads, modern portfolios, edgy web designs. 🎯 Pro tip: Use consistent margins or alignment points to keep things wild but readable.

📐 Diagonal Grid – Breaks the horizontal/vertical mold with angled lines that guide the eye with motion. 🟡 Best for: Posters, fashion layouts, album art, or anything that needs drama. ⚡️ Pro tip: Diagonals = movement. Use them to create tension or draw focus — but don’t overdo it.

🌌 Radial Grid – Elements radiate from a central point, like sunbeams. Creates focus and flow outward. 🟡 Best for: Logos, icons, event posters, spiritual or cosmic themes. 💡 Pro tip: Great for storytelling. Place key content near the center, support elements along the spokes.

➡️ Use expressive grids to amplify emotion, energy, and identity in your design.

I absolutely love fresh cherries, and what better way to enjoy them than in a cheesecake. Once you've nailed a really simple cheesecake recipe like this one (no need for gelatine), you can add in any fruit you like, which means you always have a go-to show stopping dessert, no matter the season.

Ingredients:

Biscuit base:
600g biscuits
225g butter

Filling:
625g cream cheese
400g condensed milk (you can make this from scratch-comment below if you want my recipe!)
Zest of 1 lemon
Juice 1/4 lemon
300ml cream, whipped
Juice of 10+ ripe cherries (squeezed with your fingers)

For the topping:
Two handfuls of cherries, pitted
Sprinkle of sugar
1 tsp cornflour dissolved in a tiny bit of water (optional)

30 or so cherries pitted and halved to decorate the top

Method:
Crush the biscuits until they form a fine crumb. Melt the butter and add to the crumb. Mix until combined and press into the bottom and sides of a lined 23cm cake tin. If you have too much biscuit filling and don't want a super thick base, then just use enough to cover your tin. Put in the fridge to set.

For the filling, add the cream cheese, condensed milk, lemon zest and juice to a bowl. Mix briefly until smooth and then add the juice of the cherries. Then whip the cream and add to the mixture. Fold together and then spoon into your biscuit base. Place in the fridge overnight or for 12 hours to set.

For the topping, add the cherries to a pan over a low heat with the sugar and cook until soft and juicy. Add the cornflour if you'd like it thicker. Set aside and allow to cool.

Once set, remove the cheesecake from the fridge and add the cooled cherries to the top. For the decoration, half the remaining cherries and arrange them in a circular pattern on top of the cheesecake.

text:
Recipe for Dark Chocolate Fudge with Caramel and Hazelnut Praline: 🌰🍫

Ingredients for the fudge
(Suitable for two 20 cm square rings)
This is quite a large quantity, so you can halve it
	•	6 large eggs
	•	200 grams white sugar
	•	400 grams dark chocolate (at least 70% cocoa solids)
	•	300 grams butter
	•	50 grams molasses
Alternatively – you can use 250 grams of sticky dark brown sugar instead of the white sugar and molasses
	•	120 grams high-quality cocoa powder
	•	80 grams white flour
	•	½ teaspoon salt

For the caramel toffee:
	•	100 grams sugar (½ cup)
	•	125 grams heavy cream (38% fat) – half a container
	•	A pinch of Atlantic sea salt
	•	50 grams soft butter (not melted)

For the dark chocolate praline layer:
	•	5 heaping tablespoons hazelnut praline spread (100 grams)
	•	200 grams dark chocolate
	•	80 grams butter
Optional – a pinch of sea salt

Some extra dark chocolate for decoration

⸻

How to prepare the caramel toffee:
	•	In a wide, heavy skillet over medium heat, spread the sugar evenly so there are no height differences.
	•	Caramelize the sugar – do not stir the sugar at all, only tilt the pan from side to side to distribute the heat evenly.
	•	While the sugar is caramelizing, heat the cream in the microwave so it’s hot (important! Don’t add cold cream to caramel), and soften the butter.
	•	Once the sugar is evenly colored, carefully add the hot cream while stirring vigorously until fully incorporated.
	•	Finally, blend in the butter and salt using an immersion blender.
	•	Transfer the caramel to a shallow container, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for a few hours.

⸻

After a few hours:
Preheat the oven to 180°C and line the baking tray you’re working with.

Note:
I chose to use a large flat anodized tray from which I cut circles like in the video.
You can pour the fudge directly into a round ring wrapped in aluminum foil and baking paper, but in my opinion, my method is better because it saves the trouble of wrapping each ring individually.

⸻

Preparing the fudge:
	•	In a large bowl, melt the chocolate and butter into a smooth mixture with no lumps.
	•	In another large bowl or a stand mixer, beat the whole eggs with all the sugar at once until pale and fluffy.
	•	Add the chocolate mixture to the egg mixture and stir until partially combined using a whisk.
	•	Add the molasses (if using) and the dry ingredients.
	•	At this stage, it’s recommended to switch to a spatula because the batter is very thick and might break the whisk.
	•	In any case, finish mixing with a spatula to avoid flour clumps that may have sunk and not mixed properly. Pour into the lined pan, smooth out as much as possible, pipe in the caramel, and swirl lightly with a knife.
	•	Bake for 23–25 minutes until the fudge is soft in the center but baked at the edges.
	•	Cool completely.

⸻

Once the fudge is fully cooled:
For the praline layer – melt all the ingredients in a bowl until completely smooth and glossy but not too runny.
Transfer to a convenient pouring tool/piping bag.

⸻

Assembling the dessert:
	•	Cut out circles of the desired size, and leave the fudge inside the ring without removing it.
	•	Pipe the hazelnut praline layer over each ring with fudge and smooth into a flat, glossy layer. Try not to touch it with your fingers to avoid fingerprints.
	•	Refrigerate the fudge for 20 minutes.

⸻

Decorations:
	•	While the fudge is chilling, carefully melt the chocolate in the microwave in short pulses until fully melted.
	•	Transfer the chocolate to a piping bag (preferably a small one for easier handling).
	•	After 20 minutes in the fridge, cut a very, very small hole in the piping bag to create thin, delicate lines – don’t be tempted to cut a large opening.
	•	From here, it’s up to you – you can drizzle as shown in the video or just make random lines.
	•	Finally, place halved hazelnuts and small gold leaves if you have.

text:
Studio Tour! 

Welcome to my creative space! 

It’s been very cool to be able to make records out of here for the last three + years. The space was designed by someone who really understood acoustics and cared. It definitely feels that way just listening to music in here. There are basically zero parallel walls in the entire space. Every wall is angled or treated in a way that benefits the sound. Diffusion and absorption are meticulously detailed throughout the space.

The room I work out of was actually designed for mastering. It’s a bit like wearing headphones even though the speakers are 6 feet away. 

The space also includes an iso / vocal booth that is so dead it’s nearly anechoic. A guitar booth with various amps and a Leslie. As well as a large live room that can host 6 - 10 musicians comfortably. The live room also has three different drum kits and three different pianos for various sounds/tones. A full size Steinway for the large grand sound and a felt piano for those soft movie score cuts.

Mr Fogg’s Apothecary – A whimsical cocktail bar themed like a Victorian apothecary.

The Old Operating Theatre Museum – A secret museum built in 1822 above a church.

Harry Potter Alley at Hamleys – A magical section inside the famous toy store.

Wiltons Restaurant 1742s– London’s second oldest restaurant.

Upside Down Globe – A quirky art installation.

Waterside Café at Little Venice – A charming floating café.

V&A East Storehouse – London’s newest museum.

The Pie Room at Rosewood Hotel – A unique bakery specializing in beautifully crafted British pies.

Queen’s Wood Café (N10 3JP) – A secret forest café in Highgate, surrounded by ancient woodland.

Man Inside a Clock, Paddington Station – A curious sculpture of a man suspended within a giant clock.

Barge East – A stylish boat restaurant moored in Hackney Wick.

Strawberry Hill House – An enchanting 18th-century Gothic revival castle.

The Ostler’s Hut 1860s at Lincoln’s Inn –this is London’s smallest listed building.

The Dove 1700s, Hammersmith – London’s smallest riverside pub.

House of Dreams, East Dulwich – An eccentric private home turned art installation.

Charlie & the Chocolate Factory at One Aldwych Hotel – A whimsical afternoon tea experience and factory.
